purpose: Stronger dark native editor revision after user rejected weak polished palette
prompt:
Use case: ui-mockup. Visually redesign this exact full Quader level-editor screenshot into a MUCH BOLDER, MORE FORCEFUL mature dark desktop tool. The reference is a CONTENT/GEOMETRY source, NOT a style to preserve. The user explicitly rejected its soft, polished, weak gray palette. The new visual character must be clearly different even at thumbnail size.

DESIGN INTENT:
Think early Unreal Engine 4's opinionated Slate UI and a serious professional modeling workstation. Strong graphic structure, tangible dense controls, vivid purposeful color, decisive hierarchy. Confident software built for daily production. No music aesthetics and no "rock" decoration. This is not a futuristic game launcher and not a glossy modern SaaS interface.

MAKE THESE SUBSTANTIAL CHANGES:
1. Replace EVERY softly graded dark surface with decisive FLAT COLOR BLOCKS. Main shell/splitter gutters near coal-black #08090B. Outliner, Inspector and browser wells #202124. Dock title strips and important toolbar slabs a distinctly lighter HARD GRAPHITE #414247. Header text #F0F0F2, body text #D9DADE, secondary text #A2A3AA. Keep all broad surfaces dark. No muddy close-value gray soup.
2. Make QUADER VIOLET substantial and saturated: #8045C2. Selected Outliner row is a solid confidently colored violet band with white text, NOT a washed-out gray translucent tint. Active scene tab has a solid dark-violet face with a crisp vivid-violet top edge. Pressed Object Mode and active tool controls have clear violet fills. Inactive controls are firm #36373C slabs with black separations. Purple should occupy about 4–6% of UI area, enough to give the app identity, never neon, bloom, or large decorative fields.
3. Use BURNT AMBER #E68A22 strictly as the secondary semantic color: thin active-viewport frame, selected mesh edges, small active modeling faces on tool glyphs. Conventional red/green/blue transform axes remain distinct. Small asset-folder icons use a deeper muted ochre, avoiding bright yellow chunks. This creates a strong coal/graphite/violet/amber palette rather than gray with a purple hint.
4. Make the architecture visibly heavier. Main docks have 4–6px coal-black gutters. Headers are flat full-width rectangles with a firm black lower rule. No floating cards or rounded individual Inspector section boxes; section headers and bodies form integrated native panes. Modest one-pixel highlight/shadow is acceptable ONLY on control edges; absolutely no soft lighting, vignettes, sheen, ambient gradients or blurry drop shadows on the UI.
5. Tighten and weight the typography: normal readable system sans, bold 15–17px apparent-size dock headers, 13–14px labels. No wide letter spacing, giant masthead, stencil, brush lettering or sci-fi type. Controls and fields have 0–2px corners. Numeric fields use flat medium graphite fills that clearly separate them from the panel behind. Align labels and values. Keep the X/Y/Z components STACKED for Position, Rotation and Scale.
6. Give tool icons presence: robust small shaded/solid native symbols, thicker strokes and bolder silhouettes, deliberate colors on relevant faces. Old UE4 quality rather than delicate fashionable line icons. Keep icon size useful, never huge toy buttons. Existing far-left tools become a dense strong toolbar with subtle flat block grouping, clear icon/label association and no excessive gaps.

KEEP THE FUNCTIONAL CONTENT AND SCENE:
Preserve exact Quader menus and controls from the reference; no invented features. Keep the top menu and Object Mode / Groups / Grid 32 / Angle 15° / Texture Lock controls. Keep far-left modeling tools, adjacent Outliner, central viewport, right Inspector, bottom Asset Browser. Preserve geometry and approximate camera framing of the hallway, pillars and stairs, with a selected wall and red/green/blue transform gizmo. Do not redesign the architecture, invent a game scene or add a cinematic background. The rendered geometry may have lighting; the UI chrome must be flat and forceful.
Keep the single viewport occupying the majority of the working area. Use "Hallway" for the scene tab. Populate the Outliner more believably through the existing scene hierarchy: Hallway, Floor, Walls with North wall / East wall, Columns with Column 01 / Column 02 / Column 03 / Column 04, Stairs. This changes only illustrative scene entries, not features.
Inspector keeps General, Transform with stacked X/Y/Z numeric rows, Export, Lighting, Face Texture and Layers. Asset Browser keeps the existing folder tree and ordinary asset files/material thumbnails; retain small recognizable Q file marks. Preserve the reference's actual functional labels. Only show one selected row. Keep the bottom status bar.
Use a small confident purple Q logo and "Quader — Hallway.qdr" title, no extra slogans or conceptual labels.

OUTPUT:
ONE flat full-frame desktop screenshot, widescreen around 16:9, high resolution, text sharp and legible. No external device frame, no poster border, no explanation printed on image.
DO NOT: polish it back into smooth gentle gradients; use black-on-nearly-black indecisive hierarchy; add light/cream panels; use grunge, scratches, physical material textures, metal/rivets, punk paper, stickers, gothic type, neon glow, chrome, sci-fi chamfers, glass, rounded SaaS cards, full-screen purple lighting or theme decorations. The attitude must come from firm structure, dense purposeful controls and a strong functional palette.
